Dein getreüer

Basel den 13 Jen̄nner 1717.Empf. den 6.ten Febr.

div.p:
I do not know whether to begin with congratulations or condolences. In your welcome letter you tell me how well you have begun in your new post. Yet I read it with a heavy heart at the news of your father’s death. Thus nowhere in this world is true and unalloyed joy to be found. I have this one wish: since the start of your new appointment has been clouded by such bitter sorrow, may you enjoy all the more lasting contentment in future. I am also convinced that your time at Padua will prove more rewarding than you may at first have expected. God the Lord leads his people through sorrow to joy. In any case, the troubles, hardships and sorrows of this life weigh less heavily when we can hope for a better life hereafter. If I did not know that you will be able to bear this bereavement, and that your learning and virtue will provide you with sufficient consolation, it would be my duty to sustain you against this heavy blow. May the Lord stand by you, help you where your own strength fails, and grant you future happiness to compensate for this sorrow. I also hope with all my heart that you may continue in your new post and fulfil its duties with every success, in good health and to
good purpose.

Meanwhile there has been another sorrow among your relations. Young Mr Respinger’s wife, the daughter of the salt clerk, died last night. The child had died in her womb after a fall she suffered a long time ago. She carried it until her own death, unable to give birth. It is said to be one of the most extraordinary instances of a woman carrying a child for so long. May the Most High comfort everyone who is grieving, especially the husband widowed so soon.

I thank you for the welcome account of what happened at Padua. I see from it that you can earn considerable respect once people recognise the depth of your learning. I am surprised that pedantry still reigns there so strongly, and can well imagine how hard you had to work. I have no news from here except that Mr Lindenmeyer, having had to preach at St Peter’s in place of Messrs Gernler and Huber, who are ill with gout, delivered a sermon about gout. It is a thoroughly foolish piece and is accompanied by an indecorous dialogue in verse. Write to me as often as you have time; I shall do the same. This time I can do no more than assure you that perhaps no one loves you more than

your faithful
F. Christ
Basel, 13 January 1717.
All those you greeted return your greetings.

To the most illustrious gentleman,
Mr Nicolò Bernoulli,
Professor of Mathematics,
at the Santo,
in Padua.
